newsitem.title: UK: UK's SIB, OFT approve new stock exchange rules.
newsitem.headline: UK's SIB, OFT approve new stock exchange rules.

text.p: The UK Securities and Investments Board (SIB) said on Wednesday it had approved London Stock Exchange proposals for publication of trades under the LSE's new order-driven trading system, due to start on October 20.

Separately, the Office of Fair Trading (OFT) said that none of the rules for the new Stock Exchange Electronic Trading Service (SETS) is significantly anti-competitive at present, but warned that it would keep the system under review.

SIB chairman Sir Andrew Large said in a statement, "I welcome the London Stock Exchange's proposals. The London Stock Exchange has worked with the SIB to secure the objectives of increasing transparency consistent with maintaining liquidity and avoiding losing business overseas."

Proposed publication rules for SETS will require immediate publication of all trades once completed and establish a new "worked trade" regime off the order book for very large trades of eight times normal market size or above which involve increased risk.
SETS marks a shift to a market -- initially only in FTSE 100 index stocks -- where prices are set by operators posting buy and sell orders, rather than by market makers quoting two-way prices.
The SIB said the changes would significantly improve the transparency of trading information and so make for a fairer market.

OFT Director General John Bridgeman, however, said the worked trade system still had the potential to distort competition, although not to the same extent as delayed publication of trades under the current system.

Bridgeman said it was too early to comment on the significance of any anti-competitive effects and that he would review the matter when order book trading had been running for a year, or earlier if circumstances require.

The LSE has dropped plans for mandatory interaction with the order book market, but Bridgeman also voiced concern over contingency measures the Exchange might have along these lines if it appeared necessary to "kick start" the new market.

"In my view, the least distortive way to ensure the quality of prices on SETS is to continue to strive for greater transparency across the market rather than to channel business through SETS through a regulatory solution such as mandatory interaction," he said.

For its part, the LSE welcomed the SIB report on market transparency and confirmed the parameters and publication arrangements for large trades, completing the regulatory structure for the order book market.

Under the "worked principal agreement", qualifying trades must be executed and published either when 80 percent of the risk is unwound or at the end of normal market hours on the day the agreement was entered into, whichever is the sooner.
"We will monitor the use of the worked principal agreement to ensure that it functions as intended and that the high levels of transparency we expect are maintained," the LSE said in a statement.
